body.x: Most rishta conversations cover the biography — degrees, job, height, home town — and leave the marriage itself undiscussed. Yet no marriage succeeds or struggles on biography. It succeeds or struggles on practice, money, tempers, in-laws and a hundred ordinary Tuesdays, almost all of which can be asked about in advance, kindly, if a family knows which questions carry the weight. What follows is the question bank experienced families draw on, organised by theme, with the reasoning attached — because a question asked without understanding why it matters rarely survives the politeness of a first meeting.

Practice is the foundation everything else in the house is furnished on, and it is also where polite vagueness does the most damage. The word 'religious' means something different in every home. These questions translate it into a daily routine, which is the only form in which you will actually have to live with it.

What does an ordinary weekday look like for your prayers — and what happens on the days work runs over?
How do you observe Muharram, and what would you want our home's majlis and azadari life to look like?
Which marja do you follow, and how do you settle a religious question when you are unsure of the ruling?
How do you keep Ramadan when travelling or unwell — strictly, or using the allowances?
Which part of your practice is non-negotiable for you, and where would you say you are still growing?

Listen less for the approved answers than for honesty and self-knowledge. A person who can admit a struggle plainly, without performing either piety or apology, will usually handle the harder conversations of marriage in exactly the same way.
Family life and the household you are building

Ask how their family actually runs. Who decides what, how were disagreements between their parents handled in the home they grew up in, and what do they intend to keep or deliberately change? Ask about the unglamorous work — cooking, cleaning, bills, one day the school run — not to negotiate a contract on the spot, but to discover whether the two of you are picturing the same house. Ask how much of the week they expect to spend with extended family, and how festivals, funerals and family obligations are shared between two sets of relatives. Then ask the question that reveals more than any other in this area: when you and I disagree about something serious, how should we handle it — at once, after cooling off, with a parent or elder mediating? You are not looking for a technique. You are looking for whether conflict, in their imagination, is a problem two people solve together or a contest one of them wins.
Money, children and where you will live
These three decide more of a marriage's daily happiness than romance does, and all three can be raised before nikah without indelicacy, provided both sides answer them.

How do you handle money today — saving, spending, and what you set aside for khums and charity?
Would we live on one income or two, and how do you see that changing if children arrive?
How many children do you hope for, and roughly when — and what would we do if conceiving proved difficult?
Which city, and which country, do you honestly see us in five years from now — and how fixed is that?
Is there any debt or financial commitment the other side should know about before, not after, the nikah?

The point is not to audit a stranger. It is that undisclosed debt, an unspoken plan to emigrate, or opposite assumptions about children are not small print — they are the marriage itself. Better a difficult half-hour in a family's sitting room than the same discovery in the first year, when it arrives as a betrayal instead of a fact.
The questions families forget to ask

Three subjects are routinely left unasked because each feels awkward, and each returns later with interest. The first is the in-laws' expectations: not the couple's intentions, but the parents' — how much presence, support and deference each set of parents expects from a new son- or daughter-in-law, and whether the person you are marrying actually agrees with their own parents' expectations or has simply never tested them. The second is the religious calendar as it is lived rather than believed: what Muharram will mean for your household's evenings across two months, what Ramadan will mean for work, sleep and visiting, whose family's majlis you attend and whose you host. Couples who share a faith can still be startled by how differently their childhood homes kept it. The third is relocation and care: whether either of you expects to move for work, what each of you believes you owe your parents in their old age, and where those parents will live when they can no longer manage alone. None of these questions has a correct answer. All of them have incompatible ones — which is precisely why they belong in the conversation before the yes, not in the marriage after it.
How to ask hard questions kindly

Timing and reciprocity do most of the work. Spread the questions across meetings rather than delivering an interrogation: the first meeting carries practice and direction, later meetings carry money and family detail, as trust is earned. Answer every question yourself, first or immediately after — a question you will not answer is an inspection, and people rightly resist being inspected. Ask about behaviour and plans rather than worth: 'how do you handle…' opens a door that 'are you the sort of person who…' quietly closes. And hold whatever you are told in confidence. What a person says inside a rishta conversation was said within a trust, and it stays there whatever you decide. On Shia Rishta, where messaging opens only on mutual interest and families can remain part of the process through its wali and guardian workflows, these conversations can begin in writing at a pace both households control. However they begin, the couples who ask the real questions early are the ones who eventually say yes — or no — with their eyes open.

excerpt: Biography never made a marriage work. These are the questions experienced families actually ask — on practice, money, children, in-laws and the religious calendar — and how to ask them kindly.
title: Questions to ask a potential Shia spouse before saying yes
